feed.subtitle: Building, operating, and learning in a home lab.

entry.title: AriseOne and the first repeatable jobs

link.title: AriseOne and the first repeatable jobs

entry.content:
The first thing I wanted AriseOne to do was simple: give me somewhere at home to run my own apps and keep my own data. I wanted to do it with open-source tools. Running several services made the next question obvious. How was I supposed to keep track of what each machine needed?

A script that started with a ping

The early repository has a Bash health check. It starts with a fixed list of machines. For each one, it tries a ping and then attempts to collect information like system load and free memory over SSH. The script can produce JSON as well as text. That made it possible to look at more than one machine from the same place.

The script still had a boundary. A reply to a ping didn’t tell me whether a file service was usable. It told me a machine had replied. SSH and the commands run through it were a second test, and the application would need another. That distinction shows up again later in the story, when Grafana can connect to a database but has nothing useful to display.

The Ansible playbook handled a different job. It refreshed the package cache on Debian-family systems, applied upgrades, and cleaned unused packages. At the end it looked for the reboot-required marker and reported which host needed attention. It didn’t reboot the machines. I could see where the automation stopped and where somebody still had to make a decision. These are things I can see in the January repository. I don’t have a run record that shows how often the playbook was used.

A lab with more than one job

The early February account describes the services that gave AriseOne a daily purpose. Nextcloud was the file service. Homepage was a single place to find the services. Zammad was for tickets. Proxmox ran the virtualized pieces, and a recurring problem with NVIDIA drivers turned up when the kernel changed. The notes describe a repair script and a ticket trigger. They don’t give me a full run showing that a ticket could trigger and verify a repair by itself.

The February 7 and 8 notes describe checking Zammad before changing a system and moving Markdown notes into its knowledge base. That was a way to put the past work somewhere it could be found the next time a driver or service broke. It matters here because I was learning how much of running the lab depended on having useful notes about it.

The dates in the archive don’t all mean the same thing. A later account puts the workspace setup on January 16, and the earliest repository entries I’ve reviewed are from January 20. The next build has its own log. It shows the ideas I kept working with, including Proxmox, monitoring and ticketing. It leaves open which individual services and data moved over.
entry.summary: Before CyberBiota, the lab was a collection of scripts. An inventory, a health check, and a ticket system gave those jobs a place to live.

entry.title: The failed checks stayed in the report

link.title: The failed checks stayed in the report

entry.content:
One of my October experiments was to see how much read-only diagnostic work local assistants could handle. There were two roles and a schedule. Each role had 96 windows over a day to turn the information it was given into a diagnostic result that met the check. It was a way to test repeated work rather than rely on one good answer.

The day that missed the target

One role passed in all 96 windows. The other passed in 87. That was about 91 percent against a requirement of 95 percent. The second role had missed the target even though the first had met it. An average across both roles would have hidden where the trouble was.

After a narrow correction to the handling of diagnostic data, a shorter set of scheduled checks came back clean. The first role passed 16 out of 16, and the second passed 15 out of 15. I can use that smaller result to see that the correction helped on those runs. It isn’t another full day and doesn’t replace the failures from the first one.

The decision kept the original result in the report and allowed a limited read-only diagnostic use. It did not approve full incident handling or changes to the systems the assistants were examining. That scope matters to me because the lab still hosts my own apps and data. A read that helps me investigate a problem and a change that can affect an app are two different jobs.

I wanted both sets of numbers in the blog because they explain why the work continued with a narrow scope. Anyone reading the report later can see the missed target, the follow-up, and the part of the job I was willing to rely on at that point.
entry.summary: A later clean sample helped isolate the problem. The original day still included failures, and the accepted scope stayed limited.

entry.title: The first CyberBiota build and the empty dashboard

link.title: The first CyberBiota build and the empty dashboard

entry.content:
At 11:23 p.m. on February 13, the dashboard still had empty panels. Forty-three minutes earlier, the same log had marked the work as successful. The data was in InfluxDB, and Grafana could connect to it. The screen was still empty.

I was building the first CyberBiota with Proxmox, ZFS storage, and a Linux container for the control tools. That guest ran Docker and Ansible along with InfluxDB and Grafana. Proxmox sent metrics to InfluxDB. The idea was to see what the host was doing in Grafana without having to log in and check each piece by hand. Making it work meant following the metric all the way to a panel on the screen.

What each check told me

Part of the system What the February log shows
Proxmox to InfluxDB The host sent metrics, and the database contained data.
Grafana to InfluxDB Grafana could connect. That still left the queries and dashboard to check.
Grafana panels The late check found empty panels. The log says a subsequent check found no incoming queries, and the work stopped for the night.

The next day, the fixes came in three pieces. The InfluxDB data source was changed to use explicit organization and bucket IDs. Then the dashboard JSON was cleaned up after Grafana reported a parsing error during provisioning. After that, the CPU panels needed queries that matched their actual sources. The Proxmox host metrics and the Telegraf metrics did not have the same CPU field or scale. A CPU panel that worked for one could give the wrong answer for the other.

I can’t pin the whole evening on one bug. The first note that says “success” predates the empty-panel observation. The next day’s log describes what changed, but I don’t have the original rendered panels or exact software versions to reconstruct the whole result independently. That leaves enough to tell the story without turning an early check into an uptime claim.

When I look at a dashboard now, the question I come back to is the one that was missing at 10:40 p.m.: what did the panel actually show? A sample in the database helps me narrow down a fault. The panel is what I opened the dashboard to see.
entry.summary: Proxmox was sending metrics to InfluxDB, yet Grafana showed empty panels. The next day’s corrections reveal where the checks fell short.

entry.title: Testing Dockhand before changing container management

link.title: Testing Dockhand before changing container management

entry.content:
Portainer was already there when I tried Dockhand. I wanted to see how the other tool felt for the work I usually need a management screen to do: find a container, watch its logs and check how much of the host it is using. I kept Portainer available and left the Compose deployment files in charge of configuration. That way I could compare the interfaces without having to commit to a migration.

The November 11 report is a record of what I was able to check on the first day.

Task Observation
Find what’s running Dockhand and Docker listed the same 97 containers, of which 72 were running.
Follow a container’s output A live log stream returned output from the selected container.
Check resource use Sampled memory matched Docker. CPU readings differed slightly between polls.
Try the inventory without signing in The request returned HTTP 401 after native app authentication was configured.

The report also inspected the bind mount used to reach Docker. That established the mount setting. It did not show which Docker API operations the app was authorized to make. That question needs a separate check before I can describe the permanent setup as limited to inspection.

The pilot started a planned observation period. The report I used doesn’t include the result of that period or a completed retirement of Portainer. The useful result I can show is narrower: the everyday inspection tasks worked in the comparison, and I still had the existing interface if the new one stopped being useful.
entry.summary: A November change note on the Dockhand pilot, what its checks established, and why cutover is a separate decision.

entry.title: Why CyberBiota 2 moved to bare-metal Ubuntu

link.title: Why CyberBiota 2 moved to bare-metal Ubuntu

entry.content:
The last night of the Proxmox build involved moving Linux guests to a new network, restarting them, and updating the reverse proxy so it knew where to find their services. The log says the monitoring UI remained reachable and the proxy got responses from the backends it checked. The next morning, I was starting over with Ubuntu.

That decision had a few months of experiments behind it. One March note records a failed attempt to restore OPNsense. Another describes a VyOS attempt that had problems. A later summary gives a different account of the gateway’s condition, so I can’t make a clean timeline of every working configuration. By April 6, the log does say the separate gateway experiments were being set aside in favor of Proxmox’s own network layer.

The hardest part of a network change can be getting back in when it goes wrong. The March 14 notes describe losing SSH access after a change and having limited physical recovery options on a laptop usually run without a local console. A service responding through the proxy would not help if I couldn’t reach the host to undo the change.

The April 7 rebuild

The next build, CyberBiota 2, ran Ubuntu and Docker on the hardware. The installation record names Ubuntu 25.10. It describes a separate NVMe drive for persistent application data and local model storage, and records the NVIDIA driver seeing the GPU. The reasons in the transition notes were practical: memory pressure, competing workloads, and the repeated friction of getting commands and services through nested layers.

Before After
Proxmox host with networked guests Ubuntu on the hardware, with Docker running on the host
Storage organized through the virtualization layout A separate NVMe drive allocated to persistent app and model data
Hardware and service checks spread across host and guests The native host could see the GPU in its own driver check

It was a simpler layout to describe. It also concentrated more responsibility on the one host: storage, app permissions, backups and the path back into a machine that was normally headless. The April notes don’t give me enough measurements to claim a performance improvement, or a full restore list to say every application’s data survived. Later papers refer to Ubuntu 26.04 and don’t settle whether that was an upgrade or another reinstall.

For the thing I wanted out of my lab, hosting my own apps and data, the useful part of this story is what moved where. I could keep using containers. I no longer had to put a virtualized host between that container work and every part of the machine.
entry.summary: A final Proxmox network migration was followed the next morning by a fresh Ubuntu install. That choice changed the lab’s network, storage, and hardware boundaries.

entry.title: The first backup I could show how to restore

link.title: The first backup I could show how to restore

entry.content:
If the machine disappeared, I’d need to know how to put it back together. The first CyberBiota3 backup exercise kept that question small: could I get the project repository back and read the files that explained how the lab was built?

I used Restic for a local encrypted copy. The result records both what was included and what was kept out. The project instructions and change records belonged in the backup. Known sensitive configuration and live runtime data were outside that scope. There was no reason to treat an encrypted copy as a reason to back up everything indiscriminately.

Open the copy and check it

After confirming a snapshot existed, the test restored it into a separate folder. That meant I could inspect the restored files without laying them over the working copy. The June report names the README, the operations instructions and the backup plan among the files restored. It records a separate check for excluded paths. Those are the details that let me follow the test. I can tell where the data was restored, what was expected to show up, and what the test deliberately left outside.

On July 6, the systemd timer ran the repository backup without a manual start. The receipt records an exit status of zero, a new snapshot timestamp and a successful Restic check. That’s useful because a recoverable copy today doesn’t mean the schedule will leave me another copy tomorrow. The scheduled run is also a different result from the June test, which actually put files back in a directory.

The two checks leave me with something I can work from: selected project files were recoverable, and a later backup ran on schedule. The result doesn’t tell me how to restore a live app database or bring the whole host back. And because the copy was local, it doesn’t cover losing the machine and its storage together. If I’m keeping my own data, each of those jobs deserves the same treatment as the repository: restore it somewhere safe, then check what’s really there.
entry.summary: A local encrypted snapshot, a restore into a test directory, and a later timer receipt answered different parts of the recovery question.

entry.title: The rise of CyberBiota3
entry.content:
I wanted to build my first home lab with open-source technology and use it to host my own apps and my own data.

AriseOne was where I started. I had a Proxmox host and a few scripts. One script would ping machines and try to collect health information over SSH. An Ansible playbook could apply updates to the hosts in the inventory and tell me which ones needed a reboot. By February, the lab had a file service in Nextcloud, a dashboard in Homepage and a place for tickets in Zammad. Somewhere between those scripts and those services, my work went from getting one thing online to having several things to look after.

It was time for a fresh start

That’s why I moved on from AriseOne. CyberBiota 1 and 2 were earlier versions of a lab. CyberBiota3 is where I brought together what I learned from them. The changes in the logs give that idea a physical shape.

The first CyberBiota still ran on Proxmox. It used ZFS for storage and put the monitoring tools in a Linux container of their own. The host sent data to InfluxDB, but Grafana still showed empty panels. The February log has the whole turn: “success” at 10:40 p.m., empty panels at 11:23, and work suspended at 11:34. The next day, the notes show changes to the Grafana data source, the dashboard JSON and the CPU queries. Each change fixed a different part of the path between the host and the screen.

CyberBiota 2 changed the layout. After a run of gateway and network experiments, I moved off Proxmox. The April 7 record shows a clean Ubuntu 25.10 installation, Docker on the host, a separate NVMe drive for persistent data and models, and a driver check for the GPU. Those records tell me what was installed. They don’t give me a full list of which applications or data were carried forward from AriseOne and the first CyberBiota, so I leave that part of the story open.

What I carried into CyberBiota3

By June, I still wanted the same thing: my own apps and my own data. The records now show more of the work of looking after them. When the first Compose deployment couldn’t pull two image tags, the failure stayed in the notes beside the retry. When one app needed new configuration, its database and cache were left running. When the dashboard stopped returning HTTP 500 and opened its setup screen, the result said exactly that. There wasn’t a completed setup test to put beside it yet.

The clearest example for me is the backup. A snapshot was one step. The June check restored selected project files to a separate folder and verified that important files came back. In July, a natural timer run proved that the backup could run on its own, on that occasion. If I’m going to host my own data, I want to know which of those things I have actually checked.

This blog is where I’m putting those changes in order. Start with AriseOne to see what I had to work with, or open the change journal for what’s been changing since.
entry.summary: The story of building my first open-source home lab, from AriseOne to CyberBiota3.

entry.title: A valid Compose file and a failed deployment

link.title: A valid Compose file and a failed deployment

entry.content:
I had a Compose file that passed validation and a stack that wouldn’t start. The first June 26 attempt stopped at the image pull. Two tags in the definition didn’t resolve at their registries. That left me with a perfectly readable file and software Docker couldn’t fetch.

I could check the image problem on its own. The remediation record shows the replacement tags were inspected against the registry before the next attempt. The new image names fixed that part of the deployment. They also let the apps get far enough to report problems that had nothing to do with tags.

Two apps, two different faults

Infisical was stuck restarting. The inputs it needed were supplied, but their lengths or encoding did not match what the app expected. The repair corrected the inputs and recreated the Infisical app container. Postgres and Redis were left running. The follow-up inspection showed the app running without a restart in that check. Its selected route also returned HTTP 200.

Homarr had a different problem. It returned HTTP 500 because the container was missing an encryption key that the Compose service should have passed in. Adding the mapping and recreating Homarr changed the response to HTTP 307. That sent the browser to first-run setup.

Check Result at the end of the retry
Caddy, Gitea, Infisical and n8n routes The four selected routes responded with HTTP 200.
Homarr route HTTP 307 to the setup screen, after the earlier HTTP 500.
Complete Homarr setup No completed user test in this result.

The point where I stopped for each service tells me what to try next. I would check the tags before the pull, confirm the app can start with the right configuration, and then do the thing I installed the app for. For Homarr, the next check was somebody getting through setup.

Recreating the whole stack would have made this harder to read. The evidence pointed to two apps. Keeping the database and cache in place limited what changed between checks. That’s the part I would carry into another deploy, even if the next stack used completely different software.
entry.summary: The first CyberBiota3 deployment failed before images could pull. On the retry, two applications needed different repairs.

entry.title: The webhook worked. I still rolled it back.

link.title: The webhook worked. I still rolled it back.

entry.content:
I wanted a change in Gitea to reach an n8n workflow without somebody carrying the event between the two. The pilot proved it could make the trip. It also made the sender less picky about where it could send requests and how it checked the connection. Those were the settings in use when the event arrived. The result didn’t tell me whether the integration worked under the rules I wanted to keep.

What went back

The June 30 rollback removed the webhook at the source and the associated workflow on the receiving side. It restored the transport settings that had been widened for the pilot. The follow-up checks still showed the underlying services available. I could keep Gitea and n8n without keeping that integration.

That difference is easy to lose in a journal. Writing “n8n removed” would make it look like I had taken the service out again. Writing “webhook verified” would hide the condition I wouldn’t accept. The dated rollback records enough to name both results: event delivery was demonstrated, and that particular configuration was withdrawn.

The next time I try the connection, I want to be able to show two things with the same test setup. The intended workflow received the event, and the sender reached only the intended receiver over a connection it verified. Until those two results sit next to each other, a success message is one part of the work.
entry.summary: The event arrived, but the pilot had changed the transport protections. The rollback removed the integration and kept the applications.

entry.title: Why I removed n8n and brought it back

link.title: Why I removed n8n and brought it back

entry.content:
I didn’t think n8n was useful at first. The April 8 log shows it being removed after the move to Ubuntu. I was trying local models and agent-driven work, and the workflow engine no longer looked like something I needed to keep running.

I changed my mind after reading a home lab automation article from Virtualization Howto. That’s my recollection of what brought me back to it. I can’t point to the exact example in the article that did it. What I can show is the difference between trying a tool with no clear job for it and returning to it with a job I could test.

What came back in June

n8n appears in the June 26 CyberBiota3 deployment. A route check returned HTTP 200 that day. That told me the service answered. Four days later, the webhook pilot gave it a specific task: take an event from Gitea and hand it to a workflow. Now there was a source, a trigger and a receiver that could be checked independently.

The workflow did receive the event. The way the pilot got it there loosened the connection’s safeguards, so the webhook and associated workflow were removed and the settings were restored. Both applications stayed in the lab. This is where the April and June records can be easy to confuse. April reports removing n8n. June reports deploying it and later withdrawing one connection to it. The files I reviewed do not say whether any of the April workflow data survived.

When n8n returned, the webhook finally gave me a specific way to tell whether it was doing something useful. I could also remove that one connection without undoing the rest of the installation. The rollback has its own post.
entry.summary: The April build moved toward agent-driven work. A practical home lab article made me reconsider what a visible workflow engine was good for.
